ogTitle: Camas Commons - A Regenerative Farming Land Trust
ogDescription: Pledge or donate today to help preserve 40 acres of San Juan Island farmland for perpetually affordable leases & community resilience.

sections.welcomeText: Welcome to a new model for farming. We are Ally and Guisepi, two land stewards & community enthusiasts committed to continuing on our little island’s tradition of small-scale, regenerative farming for future generations… This is Camas Commons.

sections.title: What is Camas Commons?
sections.content: Based at Talking Horse Ranch, Camas Commons is a nonprofit regenerative farming land trust being created to provide perpetually affordable residential and agricultural leases to farmers and producers on San Juan Island, WA. In a time when talented young makers and producers are priced out of life on the island, Camas Commons provides land accessibility and affordable housing for young farmers, regenerates the land, and supports the local community with healthy food and community events.

sections.title: How can I support this project?
sections.content:
Our proposal to acquire Talking Horse Ranch is due in September and the time to secure its future is now. 

We are ready to continue stewarding this land as a working farm, a place of conservation and a lasting community resource. But we cannot do it without significant financial support. 

We are seeking lead donors prepared to make transformational gifts toward the purchase of the ranch. Your support can help protect this land from speculation, keep it affordable for future farmers and producers, and preserve it in service to the community for generations to come. 

Clicking the 'PLEDGE or DONATE' button will bring you to the donation portal on our collaborating non-profit's website. 

Our first major fundraising deadline is in mid-September, when we submit our final proposal to the Land Bank. To make that proposal competitive, we need to raise $1.5 million.
It is an ambitious goal, but the opportunity is extraordinary: to secure the future of Talking Horse Ranch as protected farmland and a lasting community resource. Every contribution brings us closer—and every donor becomes part of preserving this land for generations to come.

sections.title: Learn more about Camas Commons in our FAQ below.
FAQ:

items.q: What is this land all about?
items.a:
This 120-acre farm has seen a lot — an historic dairy, an eccentric follower of the spiritual leader Ramtha, a golf course, and an organic farm. For the past 20 years, this farm has been known as Talking Horse Ranch, after the famed “talking horse” purchased by previous owner Ernie Kanzler Jr. from the channeler of his spiritual guru, Ramtha.

For these past 20-years the farm has been under-managed and kept running at a low-idle. Most of the infrastructure is in disrepair, but not beyond the point-of-no-return.

Despite all this, the land is a wonderfully magical place — with excellent topography, landscape, a seasonal creek, 6 ponds, enchanting forests, and incredibly cool and quirky buildings and landscaping. Most of the developed land is south facing slope with excellent sun, the wells produce an incredible 45 and 70 GPM, and the big barn offers 13,000 square feet of usable indoor space. These are just a few of the significant attributes.

40 of the 120 acres will be purchased for Camas Commons, with the other 80 acres entering into perpetual conservation through the San Juan Conservation Land Bank. Together, public access will be included in this plan with a walking trail that connects the Beaverton Marsh Preserve to the top of Beaver Hill, through Camas Commons.

items.q: How does this project further the Land Bank's mandate?
items.a:
The Land Bank's mandate is "To preserve in perpetuity areas in the county that have environmental, agricultural, aesthetic, cultural, scientific, historic, scenic or low-intensity recreational value and to protect existing and future sources of potable water." 

Camas Commons aligns with the Land Bank's mandate in many ways. First, creating an agricultural land trust preserves this land in perpetuity. Second, we believe that farmland isn't farmland unless it is being farmed, so this project makes sure that conserved land is actually farmed. Third, this land is beautiful, and deserves to be shared. Working with the Land Bank to make a trail across Camas Commons, and onwards to the top of Beaver Hill fulfills the low-intensity recreation and protection of aesthetic and scenic areas elements of the mandate. And finally, the water here is plentiful. We plan to diligently work towards water conservation, while also using that water to grow things to share with our community. 

This collaboration with the Land Bank finds a balance between conservation and sustainable development. For the 80 acres that the Land Bank will own, there will be no housing, and the land will be preserved for farming, recreation, and more. The 40 acres that Camas Commons will own will have the ability to have up to 4 houses and one ADU, clustered along the northern half of the property, preserving most of the existing pasture and farmland. We pledge to build housing that is low-impact, both visually and environmentally, using natural, reclaimed, and non-toxic materials.

Residential Members will have the option to own their own home and sign a 99-year lease, or lease a home from the nonprofit. They, and Non-Residential Members, will have the opportunity to lease land, infrastructure, or buildings with short-term leases for agricultural, traditional craft, forestry, or other sustainability-related endeavors.

items.q: How can I get a lease at Camas Commons?
items.a: Applications for residential leases will open within a year of the purchase of the land. Agricultural leases may open sooner than that. If you want to be on a list, please contact us at info@camascommons.org

items.q: How many people will live at Camas Commons?
items.a: Based on the allowed density, four houses plus the existing ADU are permissible. Averaging 2-4 people per house, we see 10-20 full time residents (including children). At least one member from each house must be involved in agriculture, sustainability-adjacent activities, or an administrative role.

items.q: What will this project offer the local community?
items.a: Members of Camas Commons will be producing agricultural products, like fruits, vegetables, eggs, meat, and more, as well as useful and traditional crafts and land-connection events. There will also be activities like educational workshops, seasonal gatherings, petting zoos, live music, a farm store and more.

Current Talking Horse Ranch land stewards Guisepi Spadafora and Ally Rugge have been helping facilitate a path towards this goal for the past several years. Guisepi grew up on the island, and after years of service-based travel (i.e. the Free Tea Bus [freeteaparty.org](https://freeteaparty.org)), returned to the islands with his now wife, Ally, to find the right piece of land to dedicate themselves to. He has 20 years of experience in the nonprofit world, and loves to tinker. Ally has lived and worked on Talking Horse Ranch three times in the past 15 years, learning to grow food, rehabilitate soil, and raise chickens and dairy goats ([women-who-stare-at-goats-collective](https://www.visitsanjuans.com/account/women-who-stare-at-goats-collective)). They got married on the farm in 2023.

Raised on San Juan Island, Guisepi Spadafora has long dreamed of returning home to help steward a place that could nourish both the land and the community. After years of service-based travel—including his work with the Free Tea Bus([freeteaparty.org](https://freeteaparty.org))—he returned to the islands with his now wife, Ally Rugge, to find a place where they could put down roots and dedicate themselves to a larger public vision.

For Ally, that place has long been Talking Horse Ranch. Over the past 15 years, she has lived and worked on the farm three different times, growing food, restoring soil, and raising chickens and dairy goats through the Women Who Stare at Goats Collective. ([women-who-stare-at-goats-collective](https://www.visitsanjuans.com/account/women-who-stare-at-goats-collective))

Stewardship is something that comes naturally for Ally & Guisepi, and being in service to the community they surround themselves with has been at the core of their relationship. Together, they bring 40 years of combined experience in nonprofit and service-based endeavors. Guisepi has also been a volunteer for the Land Bank. He also has a love of building, salvaging, repairing, and finding creative solutions. 

Ally is a Sociologist and works as a counselor & initiation mentor for young women. She developed two curriculums that offer guidance for significant life changes & chapters within the experience of womanhood in order to support the natural maturation that each stage entails. Although her work with animals is more recent, she has found her skills as a counselor seems to extend effortlessly to animals. This has informed her work in developing what she calls, Animal Midwifery, as a method of raising animals that she says is ‘farming with a feminine touch.’
For almost 4 years, they have been care-taking Talking Horse Ranch, where they got married in 2023. Today, they are working to help preserve the land and carry its legacy forward—as a working farm, a community resource, and a place rooted in stewardship, connection, and possibility.

items.q: How can I support Camas Commons?
items.a:
Please consider pledging or donating money to our cause. All pledges will only be collected if our proposal is chosen and we make our fundraising goals.

Our donate button will take you to the website of our collaborating non-profit, On Sacred Ground Land Trust.
